unit.title: Perform advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping

summary: This Level 3 unit covers advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping. You will learn to choose between oxy-fuel, air carbon arc, plasma and grinding for each job; to set up and use air carbon arc, oxy-fuel and plasma gouging; to back gouge welds and dig out defects for repair; to cut bevels, pipe saddles, branch holes and template shapes; and to check cut quality, control the effects of heat, plan the job, protect the team and supervise others.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 3 qualification (MEM30215). It covers **advanced manual thermal cutting, gouging and shaping**: choosing the right thermal process for a job; air carbon arc gouging, oxy-fuel gouging and washing, and plasma gouging; back gouging welds and digging out defects for repair; cutting edge preparations; cutting pipe saddles and branch holes; shaping parts with templates; and checking, recording and supervising the work.

Gouging removes metal fast, but it is one of the most hazardous jobs in the shop: a jet of molten metal, very loud noise, heavy fume, high current and a real fire risk. At Level 3 you are expected to plan these jobs, set them up, do them well and lead others safely.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 3 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other providers, and fabricators, boilermakers and maintenance welders who prepare and repair heavy welded work.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Choose the process
Pick oxy-fuel, air carbon arc, plasma or grinding for each cutting or gouging job, and explain why.
Plan the job
Work out time, electrodes, gas and air; check that the power source, compressor and gas supply can last the job; plan the order of work.
Work safely and protect others
Control molten metal, fire, noise, fume, arc light, shock and gas hazards; set up a safe area; wear full PPE.
Gouge
Set up and use air carbon arc, oxy-fuel and plasma gouging to make clean, even grooves of the right depth and shape.
Back gouge and remove defects
Gouge weld roots to sound metal, dig out cracks and other defects for repair, and remove temporary attachments without harming the job.
Cut edge preparations
Cut bevels, root faces, and J and U grooves, by hand and with a cutting trolley.
Cut and shape pipe and plate
Mark and cut pipe saddles and branch holes, cut shapes with templates, and control distortion.
Inspect and record
Check cut faces and grooves against the drawing, the WPS and the quality standard; record repairs and results.
Supervise
Brief, demonstrate, supervise and assess less experienced team members.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on choosing the process, safety, set-up, gouging technique, electrodes, back gouging, defect removal, oxy-fuel and plasma gouging, edge preparation, pipe cutting, templates, cut quality, planning and records.

A **written paper**: short answers that need exact terms (for example saddle, back gouging, J groove, included angle, stick-out, jointed electrodes, scarfing, double-V) and essays in full sentences, with any sums worked out.

**Practical tasks** done as a group: back gouge a butt joint and dig out a marked defect, with a method plan and repair records; and develop and cut a pipe branch saddle and its hole and flame bevel a pipe end, with an inspection record.

blocks.note: Learn the reasons, not only the steps. Many questions ask why: why gouge downwards on a vertical joint, why slope the ends of a repair groove, why grind after air carbon arc gouging, why use plasma on stainless steel.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Each thermal process removes metal in a different way, so each suits different metals and jobs.

head: Process
How it removes metal
Metals
Best for
Limits
rows: Oxy-fuel cutting
A preheat flame heats the steel to its ignition temperature (bright red); a jet of pure oxygen then burns the iron and blows the oxide out of the cut (kerf)
Carbon and low-alloy steels
Cutting plate and sections to size, bevelling, pipe cutting, thick steel; needs no electricity
Will not cut stainless steel, aluminium, copper alloys or cast iron
Oxy-fuel gouging and washing
The same burning action, with a gouging or washing nozzle held at a low angle, so the oxygen scoops out a groove instead of cutting through
Carbon and low-alloy steels
Grooves; removing weld reinforcement, backing strips, rivet and bolt heads
As above; heats a wider area than arc gouging
Air carbon arc gouging (ACAG, also called CAC-A)
An arc from a copper-coated carbon electrode melts the metal and a jet of compressed air blows it away
Most metals, including cast iron
Back gouging; digging out defects and old welds; fast removal on steel and cast iron
Very noisy, heavy fume and a molten-metal jet
Leaves a carbon-rich surface that must be ground off
Poor for cutting plate to size: wide, rough cut, many electrodes used
Plasma cutting and gouging
A narrow, extremely hot arc in a jet of gas (often compressed air) melts the metal and blows it out
Any metal that conducts electricity
Cutting stainless steel and aluminium; gouging where carbon must not be left behind
Needs power and clean, dry air or gas; consumables wear; very high open-circuit voltage
Grinding
An abrasive disc wears the metal away
Any
Small or shallow defects, thin or finished parts, cleaning up gouged grooves
Slow for large amounts of metal

blocks.note: Oxy-fuel cutting works only when the metal **burns** in oxygen and its oxide melts at a lower temperature than the metal, so the oxide can be blown out. Stainless steel (chromium oxide) and aluminium (aluminium oxide) form oxides that melt far hotter than the metal itself, so they melt but do not burn away. Cast iron melts before it reaches its ignition temperature.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Matching the process to the job

head: Job
Usual best choice
Why
rows: Back gouging long roots on thick carbon steel
Air carbon arc
Fast, with good control of depth
Removing a crack from a cast iron machine base
Air carbon arc, then grinding
Oxy-fuel cannot gouge cast iron
Gouging stainless steel or aluminium
Plasma gouging or grinding
No carbon is left in the surface; oxy-fuel will not work
Removing rivet heads or a backing strip on steel
Oxy-fuel washing
Removes metal close to the surface with a broad, controllable heat
A small, shallow defect on a thin or finished part
Grinding
Least heat, no carbon, no risk of burning through
Cutting plate to size and bevelling
Oxy-fuel (thick carbon steel) or plasma (thinner steel, stainless, aluminium)
A clean, narrow kerf; arc gouging gives a wide, rough cut and wastes electrodes

head: Hazard
What can happen
Controls
rows: Molten metal and sparks
Air carbon arc gouging blows a jet of molten metal several metres; sparks travel 10 m or more and fall through gaps. Burns, fires, and damp concrete bursting when hot metal hits it.
Aim the molten stream into a clear zone, away from people, cylinders, hoses, cables and anything that burns
Keep it off damp concrete: cover the floor with steel plate or work over dry sand
Fire-resistant screens and blankets
Extinguisher at hand; fire watch during and after the work
Noise
Air carbon arc gouging is very loud, often above 100 dB(A): enough to damage hearing quickly
Ear plugs **and** ear muffs together
Warn and protect people nearby
Limit the time each person gouges
Fume
Gouging makes a lot of fume fast: iron and copper oxides, plus chromium and nickel from stainless steel, zinc from galvanising and lead from old paint
Local fume extraction at the work
Keep your head out of the plume
Respirator where extraction is not enough
Remove coatings first
Arc light
Burns to eyes and skin, for you and for people nearby
Helmet with the shade the chart gives for the current (often about shade 12 for air carbon arc gouging up to about 500 A)
Screens
Clear safety glasses under the helmet
Electric shock
High currents, long leads, wet sites; plasma sets have a very high open-circuit voltage (often over 250 V)
Dry PPE and gloves
Leads and torch checked; a torch with cracked insulation taken out of use
Plasma: switch off before changing consumables; never bypass the safety interlocks
Stray welding current
Current passing through bearings, hinges, chains or lifting gear can arc and damage them
Fix the return clamp to the job, close to the area being gouged
Gas cylinders and flashback
Fire or explosion from leaks, flashback, or oil on oxygen fittings
Cylinders upright and chained
Flashback arrestors at the regulators and check valves at the torch
Leak-test the joints
No oil or grease on oxygen equipment
Containers and confined spaces
Vapour left in drums and tanks explodes; leaked oxygen makes clothing burn fiercely; fuel gas or fume builds up
Never cut or gouge a container that held flammables until it is cleaned and declared gas-free
Confined-space permit and gas testing
Never ventilate with oxygen

flow: Agree the time and place with the supervisor and other trades; get a hot-work permit if the workplace uses them
Choose a position where the molten metal will be thrown into a clear zone
Remove or cover anything that can burn; move cylinders and hoses well away; protect damp concrete
Put up fire-resistant screens and warning signs
Set up fume extraction at the work
Fix the return clamp close to the gouging area; route cables and air hoses where nobody will trip
Put a charged extinguisher at hand and name a fire watcher
After the work: stubs in a metal container; check for smouldering material during and after, for at least 30 minutes or as the permit says

ul: Helmet with the right shade, with clear safety glasses underneath.
Fire-resistant jacket or leathers, leather gauntlet gloves, a fire-resistant cap, and trousers worn over the boots so molten metal cannot drop inside.
Ear plugs and ear muffs.
Respirator as the risk assessment says.
**Overhead work:** leather cape or sleeves and a closed collar; stand to one side so molten metal falls past you, never directly under the joint.

blocks.note: On outdoor jobs, watch the wind. By day the sea breeze usually blows inland from the coast; it carries fume, sparks and molten spray with it. Set up so the wind takes them away from people and buildings, and in the dry months clear dry grass and bush, which catch fire easily. In an emergency, dial 110 for fire and ambulance.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Oxy-fuel cutting: refresher and cut quality

blocks.p: Advanced work such as bevelling, pipe cutting and gouging builds on sound oxy-fuel cutting. The cut is only as good as the set-up.

head: Point
Acetylene
LPG (propane or propane-butane)
rows: Flame temperature
Hottest, about 3 100 °C
Cooler, about 2 800 °C
Preheating and piercing
Fast
Slower
Oxygen used
Less
Several times as much as acetylene
Equipment
Acetylene nozzles, regulators, hoses and arrestors
LPG nozzles (often two-piece) and LPG-rated regulators, hoses and arrestors
Special limits

Never used above about 1 bar (15 psi), the usual safe limit. Draw no more than about one-seventh of a cylinder's contents per hour (some suppliers say one-tenth for long use); larger nozzles need cylinders joined on a manifold.
Heavier than air: leaks collect in pits and drains

blocks.note: LPG is easy to get in Jamaica and cheaper to run, so many shops cut with oxygen and LPG. Use the nozzles, regulators and flashback arrestors made for LPG, never acetylene parts, and expect a slower start.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Cylinders upright and chained; the right regulator on each gas
Flashback arrestors at the regulators and check valves at the torch
Hoses undamaged, the right colours and correctly fitted
Nozzle the right type and size for the gas and the thickness (from the maker's chart); its holes clean, using tip cleaners of the right size
Pressures set from the chart; joints leak-tested with leak-detection fluid
Light up and shut down in the order the maker and the Centre give (in many workshops the fuel gas valve is closed first, then the oxygen)

ul: Clean heavy mill scale, rust and paint off the cut line: they slow the start and spoil the cut.
Support the plate so the off-cut can fall freely, without pinching the nozzle or dropping on your feet.
Hold the preheat cones just clear of the surface; heat the edge to bright red, then open the cutting oxygen and travel at a steady speed.

To pierce, preheat a spot in the waste, open the oxygen slowly while lifting the nozzle a little so the blown-back slag cannot block it, then lower it to cutting height. On thick plate, start from an edge or a drilled hole instead.

blocks.p: A thermally cut face is graded mainly on its **squareness** (how far the face is out of square) and its **surface roughness**, against the cut quality standard the job names. The **drag lines** on the face also show how the cut went.

head: What you see
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Clean face, near-vertical drag lines, sharp top edge, little dross that knocks off easily
Correct settings
Keep them and record them
Drag lines curving strongly backwards; bottom corners not cut through; the cut may be lost
Travel too fast
Slow down
Rough, gouged face; heavy dross stuck underneath
Travel too slow, or oxygen pressure wrong
Speed up; check the pressure against the chart
Top edge rounded, with beads of melted metal
Preheat flame too strong, or nozzle too close to the plate
Reduce the preheat; set the nozzle height
Wavy, irregular face with notches
Dirty or damaged nozzle, unsteady travel, or oxygen pressure too high
Clean or replace the nozzle; use a guide or trolley; set the pressure
Bevelled or out-of-square face
Nozzle tilted, or too high
Hold the nozzle square at the right height

head: Part
What you need to know
rows: Power source

A DC constant-current welding machine (or engine-driven welder) able to give the gouging current for long spells: check its duty cycle at that current. For steel, gouging is normally done on **DCEP** (electrode positive).
Torch
Jaws grip the electrode; air holes in the jaws blow air along the electrode; an air valve on the handle; the head turns so the air jets can be set on the side of the electrode facing the work.
Electrodes

Carbon-graphite rods with a thin copper coat, which helps carry the current and slows the wear. Round (most common), flat (rectangular) for removing reinforcement and leaving a flat surface, and **jointed** electrodes with a socket and peg so a new one fits onto the stub.
Air supply

Compressed air, typically about 550–690 kPa (80–100 psi) at the torch, with enough **flow** for the torch and electrode size. A pressure gauge on the compressor does not show flow: check the pressure at the torch while air is flowing.
Return clamp
On the job, close to the gouging, so current cannot pass through bearings, hinges or chains.

head: Round copper-coated electrode
Typical DCEP current (always use the maker's chart)
rows: 4.0 mm
about 90–150 A
4.8 mm
about 150–200 A
6.4 mm
about 200–400 A
8.0 mm
about 250–450 A
9.5 mm
about 350–600 A

blocks.p: **Current too low:** the arc is unstable, the electrode sticks, and carbon is left in the groove. **Current too high:** the electrode burns away fast, glows red well back from the arc, and its copper coat strips back.

flow: Check the permit, the area, the clear zone, the return clamp and your PPE
Fit the electrode with a stick-out of up to about 150 mm (or as the maker says), with the air jets on the side facing the work
Set the current from the maker's chart and the polarity (DCEP for steel)
Open the air valve **before** you strike the arc
Touch the electrode lightly on the work at the start of the groove and draw it back to a short arc; do not let it touch again
Hold the electrode at a steady angle (often about 35–45° to the surface), pointing the way you are travelling, and push forward at a steady speed
Watch the groove and keep the angle, speed and arc length steady
Stop by pulling the electrode away; when it has burned back to about 50–75 mm, stop and reset the stick-out

head: To get ...
Do this
rows: A deeper groove
Steeper electrode angle and slower travel (within the current range)
A shallower, smoother groove
Flatter angle and faster travel
A wider groove
A larger electrode (the groove is usually a little wider than the electrode), or a slight side-to-side movement
A groove deeper than one pass can safely make
Two or more passes, each cleaning out the last; never hold the electrode still or push it into the metal

ul: **Flat** is easiest and gives the best control.
**Vertical:** gouge **downwards**, so gravity carries the molten metal down and away from the groove.
**Horizontal:** gouge so the molten metal falls away from the groove and from you.
**Overhead:** use a lower current or smaller electrode, angle the electrode so the metal falls clear, wear full leathers, and stand to one side.

blocks.h: Faults in air carbon arc grooves

head: Fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Shiny black carbon deposits in the groove
The electrode touched the work (arc too short or pushed in), or the current is too low
Keep a short arc without touching; set the current to the chart; grind the deposits out before welding, as carbon can make the weld crack
Molten metal and slag left in the groove
Air pressure or flow too low, air valve not fully open, or air jets on the wrong side
Check the compressor, hose and torch; set the jets on the work side; open the valve fully
Electrode glowing red far back; copper stripping back
Current too high for the electrode size, or too much stick-out
Set the current to the chart, or use a larger electrode; reset the stick-out
Electrode sticking; unstable arc
Current too low, or the electrode touching the work
Raise the current within the chart; keep the arc gap
Uneven, wavy groove
Unsteady hand, uneven speed or changing angle
Brace your arm and body; practise on scrap at an even speed
Narrow, deep groove with a sharp bottom
Electrode angle too steep and travel too slow
Flatter angle, faster travel, or a larger electrode

blocks.note: After air carbon arc gouging, the groove surface is rich in carbon and may be hard. Always grind it to bright metal before welding, as well as removing any carbon deposits.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Oxy-fuel gouging, washing, scarfing and plasma gouging

ul: A **gouging nozzle** is curved or bent and has a large oxygen bore that gives a wide, low-speed oxygen stream.

**To start:** heat a spot at the start of the groove to bright red with the nozzle held fairly steep, then open the gouging oxygen and lower the nozzle to a low angle to the plate (follow the nozzle maker's guide; often about 15–30°).
Because the nozzle is held at a **low angle**, the oxygen stream scoops out a groove instead of cutting a kerf through the plate.
Depth is controlled by the nozzle angle, the travel speed and the oxygen: steeper and slower gives a deeper groove.
Gouging nozzles use a lot of fuel gas; with acetylene, check the withdrawal limit and use a manifold if needed.

blocks.p: **Washing** removes metal standing on the surface (rivet heads, bolt heads, weld reinforcement, backing strips) without cutting into the plate underneath. A washing (rivet-washing) nozzle is held almost **parallel** to the plate: heat the head, then let the oxygen wash it off; the rivet shank is then punched out.
**Scarfing** removes a thin surface layer of metal to take out surface defects such as seams and shallow cracks, using a scarfing nozzle at a low angle (or, in steel mills, a scarfing machine).

ul: A **gouging tip** (and its matching shield) is fitted to the plasma torch in place of the normal cutting tip.
The torch is held at a shallow angle with a short stand-off, as the maker's guide says; depth is set by the angle, the speed and the current.
It leaves **no carbon** behind and works on any conductive metal, so it is the usual choice for gouging stainless steel and aluminium.
It is generally quieter and makes less smoke than air carbon arc gouging, but it still needs full PPE, screens and extraction.
Plasma sets work at a very high open-circuit voltage: switch off at the set before changing tips, and never defeat the torch's safety switch.

blocks.p: Double-sided butt joints (double-V, double-bevel) are welded from one side first. The root of that first weld often has lack of fusion, slag or incomplete penetration. **Back gouging** removes the root from the other side down to sound weld metal, so the second-side weld fuses onto clean, sound metal and the joint has full penetration.

flow: Read the WPS: any preheat, the gouging method, the groove shape, and how the gouged root must be checked
Set up the station and the safe area; preheat if the WPS says
Gouge along the root in one or more passes until sound weld metal is reached
Keep a smooth **U-shaped** groove, wide enough for the welder to reach and fuse the bottom, with gently sloped ends
Grind the groove to bright metal
Inspect it: no slag lines, dark root lines or cracks; use dye penetrant (PT) or magnetic particle testing (MT) if the specification asks
Record what was found and the inspection result, then weld it promptly, before it rusts or loses its preheat

ul: A **V-shaped groove with a sharp bottom** traps slag and leaves lack of fusion, because the welder cannot reach or fuse the bottom.
If you find a defect running deeper (a line of slag, a crack), keep gouging until it has all gone, then check and record it. Never weld over it.
On long seams, gouge and weld in sections in a planned, balanced order: the groove does not stand open to rust and dirt, preheat is easier to keep, and distortion is controlled.

blocks.h: Digging out a defect for repair

flow: Report the defect and get an approved repair procedure (essential on structural, pressure and lifting work)
Clean the area and find the true extent of the defect with PT or MT; cracks are often longer than they look. Mark both ends.
If the procedure asks, drill a small **stop hole** just beyond each end of a crack, so it cannot run further while it is removed
Preheat as the procedure says (thick or high-strength steel, cast iron): fast cooling of the gouged surface could harden it and start new cracks
Gouge along the defect in shallow passes until it has all gone, continuing past each end as the procedure says
Leave a smooth U-groove with **gently sloped ends**, so the welder can fuse the repair at the ends
Grind the groove clean, then check again with PT or MT to prove no defect is left
Measure and record the location, length, depth and width; pass it for welding
After the repair weld, inspect again (and carry out any NDT the specification requires)

ul: Check the drawing or procedure for how lugs, cleats and strongbacks are to be removed, and whether preheat is needed.
Make sure the attachment carries no load, and that the job is safe for hot work (a tank must be clean and gas-free).
Cut or gouge the attachment off a few millimetres **clear of** the surface, never into it.
Grind what is left flush, without grinding below the surface of the plate.
Check for nicks and thinning (with a straight edge, and a thickness gauge if in doubt) and for cracks (PT or MT), as the specification says.
Repair any defect by an approved method, record the work, and restore the coating.

blocks.p: A repair record gives: the job and joint or location; the defect type and size; the method used; the length, depth and width removed; the inspection results before welding; the repair WPS and welder; the final inspection and NDT results; and the names and dates. A repaired weld is not the same as a new one: it must be traceable.

sections.title: Edge preparation, pipe cutting and shaping

head: Preparation
Where used
Points to know
rows: Single-V
Butt joints welded from one side
Bevel about 30° on each plate gives a 60° **included angle**; root face about 1–2 mm; follow the WPS
Double-V (X)
Thick plate welded from both sides
Needs about half the weld metal of a single-V, and the shrinkage on the two sides balances; the root is usually back gouged
Single bevel / double bevel (K)
Tee and corner joints
Bevel on the web plate only; a double bevel on thick plate needs less weld metal and balances the shrinkage
J and U
Very thick plate
A J has one curved side and one straight side (on one plate of a tee or corner joint); a U has both sides curved. They need less weld metal, but are harder to make (machined or gouged).

ul: **Bevel angle**: the angle cut on one plate. **Included angle**: the total angle between the two bevelled faces. **Root face**: the flat, unbevelled land at the root. **Root gap**: the space between the parts at the root.
Too small an angle: poor access and lack of fusion. Too large: extra weld metal, time and distortion. Too big a root face: incomplete penetration.
By hand, run the nozzle against a straight-edge guide at the bevel angle.

A **cutting trolley** carries the torch along a track at a steady speed: one torch for a plain bevel; **two torches** (one upright for the root face, one angled for the bevel) for a bevel and root face in one pass; **three torches** (one upright and two angled opposite ways) for a double bevel with a root face in one pass.
Make a trial cut to set the speed and angle, then clean off the slag and grind the faces bright.

Check the bevel angle with a bevel gauge or protractor, the root face with a rule or gauge, and the edge for straightness and notches. If an angle is outside the WPS tolerance, grind it into tolerance and check again. Record the results.
Mark a true square line round the pipe with a **wrap-around** (a flexible band wrapped round the pipe, edges lined up), and mark the four centre lines (quarter lines).

A **saddle** (fish-mouth) is a pipe end cut to fit onto the curved side of another pipe. Develop its shape from the two pipe sizes (by drawing, or using a template the Centre has checked), cut the template from card or thin sheet, wrap it round the branch on the square line, and mark round it.
Centre punch the marks so they are not burnt away by the cut.
Large pipe is cut by hand in sections (often quarters), turning the pipe between them, so the torch can always be held at the right angle in a comfortable position.
For a square cut, keep the torch pointing towards the centre of the pipe; for a bevel, tilt it to the bevel angle.

head: Branch type
How it fits
Hole in the main pipe
rows: Set-on
The branch sits on top of the main pipe
About the **bore** (inside diameter) of the branch; cut with the torch pointing towards the centre of the main
Set-in (set-through)
The branch passes through the wall of the main
About the **outside diameter** of the branch, cut with the torch kept parallel to the branch centre line so the branch can pass through

blocks.p: Pierce in the waste (the middle of the hole) and work out to the line. Clean off the slag, grind to the line, and check the fit: an even gap all round, the branch square in both directions, and the bevel and root face as the WPS says.

When a hand torch is run against a template, the cut lies a set distance from the template's edge: the **offset**, from the template edge to the centre of the cut, allowing for half the kerf. Work it out from a trial cut. For an **outside shape**, make the template smaller than the part by the offset on every edge; for a **hole**, make it larger.

head: Example
Working
Template size
rows: Gusset 300 mm × 200 mm, offset 12 mm

ul: Make the template from steel sheet or flat bar stiff enough not to warp; check it against the drawing and mark it with the job number.
Lay out (nest) the parts on the plate to use it well, leaving room for the kerf.
Clamp the template firmly; keep the nozzle height and angle steady.

Cut **inside features first** (holes, slots) while the part is still held by the plate, then the outside. For a slot, pierce or drill a hole at each end, then cut between them: the ends come out clean and round.
Check the first part fully against the drawing, then each part against a master part or template, with a full check at regular intervals. Mark and set aside any out of tolerance.
A long, narrow strip heated along one edge **bows**. Cut both edges at the same time with two torches, or leave short uncut **tabs** (bridges) and cut them last.
Start strips and shapes from a drilled or pierced hole rather than the plate edge where the drawing allows.
Plan the cutting order so the parts stay held in the plate skeleton as long as possible; clamp the plate.

sections.title: Effects of heat, planning and supervision

blocks.h: How the heat affects the steel

head: Effect
Why it happens
Prevention
rows: Hard, brittle cut or gouged edges that can crack (for example when bent)
On high-carbon, high-strength or thick steel, the edge is heated fast and then cooled fast by the cold plate around it
Preheat as the procedure says; grind off the hardened layer before welding or bending
Carbon pick-up from air carbon arc gouging
A thin, carbon-rich layer and carbon deposits are left in the groove
Steady arc without touching; grind the groove clean; on stainless steel use plasma or grinding, as carbon lowers its corrosion resistance
Distortion
Uneven heating and cooling
Clamping, balanced cutting and gouging, two-torch cuts, tabs, a planned sequence
Coarse grain
Holding the steel very hot for a long time
Keep the heat local and keep moving

head: Check
How to work it out
Worked example
rows: Electrodes
Length to gouge ÷ length gouged per electrode, plus spares
9.6 m at 320 mm per electrode = 30 electrodes; with 10% spare, 33
Arc time
Length ÷ travel speed
8 m at 400 mm/min = 20 minutes of arc time
Working time
Arc time ÷ the share of time the arc is actually on
If the arc is on 40% of the time: 20 ÷ 0.4 = 50 minutes
Acetylene supply
Nozzle consumption ÷ the most each cylinder can give per hour
A cylinder holding 7 700 litres gives at most about 1 100 litres an hour (one-seventh); a nozzle using 1 800 litres an hour needs 2 cylinders on a manifold
Air
The torch's air flow at the electrode size, against the compressor's delivered flow
Check the pressure at the torch with air flowing; on site, plan a portable compressor with enough flow, placed clear of the fume
Power source
The gouging current, and how long each spell lasts, against the duty cycle
A machine rated well below the gouging current, or with a low duty cycle at it, will cut out or be damaged

blocks.note: Plan rotation: gouging is hot, loud and tiring. Share it out, so nobody gouges for hours at a stretch, and give people breaks out of the heat.
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Brief the hazards, the controls and the PPE, including hearing protection and a fire-resistant cap
Show the set-up: polarity, current from the chart, air supply, jets on the work side, stick-out, and where the molten metal will go
Demonstrate a groove on scrap while they watch from a safe place with suitable eye protection
Let each person set up and gouge on scrap while you stand beside them, ready to stop the work
Check their position, angle, speed and arc length, and the groove's depth, evenness and carbon; give short, clear feedback after each run
Let them gouge on a job only when their grooves are consistently good; record their progress and sign off what they can do

ul: One person per gouging booth or screened area: each gouger needs room, screens and a safe direction for the molten metal.
Stop any unsafe work at once, and explain why.
**Method plan**: process, electrode size and current, polarity, air, order of work, safe direction for the molten metal, PPE, fire precautions, inspection.
**Repair records** for every defect removed and repaired.
**Inspection records** for bevels and fit-up: angle, root face, gap, squareness.
Permits, and any incidents or near misses.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise with your instructor.

ul: I can choose between oxy-fuel, air carbon arc, plasma and grinding for a cutting or gouging job, and explain why.
I can explain why oxy-fuel will not cut stainless steel, aluminium or cast iron.
I can set up a safe gouging area and protect myself and others from molten metal, fire, noise, fume, arc light and shock.
I can set up an oxy-fuel set for LPG or acetylene, and read a cut face to correct the speed, preheat and nozzle height.
I can set up air carbon arc gouging: power source, polarity, electrode, current, air and stick-out.
I can gouge a smooth groove of the right depth in the flat, vertical, horizontal and overhead positions.
I can name air carbon arc gouging faults and their causes, and put them right.
I can explain and use oxy-fuel gouging, washing, scarfing and plasma gouging.
I can back gouge a weld root to sound metal, and check and record the groove.
I can dig out a defect for repair and remove a temporary attachment without harming the job.
I can explain and cut single-V, double-V, bevel, J and U preparations, and check them against the WPS.
I can mark and cut pipe saddles and set-on and set-in branch holes.
I can make and use a template with the right offset, and control distortion when cutting.
I can explain how cutting and gouging heat affects steel, and how to prevent the problems.
I can plan a gouging job: electrodes, time, gas, air and power.
I can brief, supervise and assess less experienced team members, and keep the records.

terms: Removing metal with an arc from a copper-coated carbon electrode and a jet of compressed air
Removing the root of a weld from the back, so the second side can be welded onto sound metal
The angle cut on one plate / the total angle between the two bevelled faces
The area kept free of people and anything that can burn, into which the molten metal is thrown
A shiny black lump of carbon left in a groove when the electrode touches the work
A carriage that carries a cutting torch along a track at a steady speed for straight and bevel cuts
A butt joint bevelled on both sides of each plate, like two Vs point to point
The curved lines on a thermally cut face that show the speed and quality of the cut
Oxide and metal stuck to the bottom edge of a cut
The part fitted to a plasma torch in place of the cutting tip for gouging
Grooves with one curved side (J) or two curved sides (U), used on very thick plate
Carbon electrodes with a socket at one end and a peg at the other, so a new one fits onto the stub
The distance from a template's edge to the centre of the cut, allowing for half the kerf
The flat, unbevelled land at the root of a joint preparation
A pipe end cut to fit onto the curved side of another pipe
Removing a thin surface layer of metal to take out defects such as seams or cracks
A branch sitting on top of the main pipe / passing through its wall
The length of carbon electrode sticking out beyond the torch jaws
A small hole drilled just beyond the end of a crack to stop it running
Removing rivet heads, bolt heads or reinforcement flush with the surface, with a nozzle held almost parallel to the plate
A flexible band wrapped round a pipe to mark a true square line

c1.title: A cracked hopper at a quarry near Bog Walk
c1.text: Romaine is to remove a crack in a welded corner of a 20 mm carbon steel hopper at a limestone quarry near Bog Walk, St Catherine, so that it can be repaired. He has a DC welding machine, an air carbon arc torch, 8 mm copper-coated electrodes (maker's chart 250–450 A) and the quarry's compressor. The repair procedure asks for dye penetrant (PT) checks, preheat to 100 °C, and grinding of the gouged groove before welding. The crack that can be seen is about 120 mm long.

c2.title: A fishing boat hull at Alligator Pond
c2.text: Fabian is gouging out a cracked weld on the 8 mm steel hull of a fishing boat drawn up on the beach at Alligator Pond, Manchester. The compressor stands on a truck about 40 m away, feeding a long, small-bore air hose; when he starts gouging, slag and molten metal stay in the groove. His welding machine is a 200 A generator set, and he has brought 8 mm electrodes (maker's chart 250–450 A). A sea breeze is blowing from the boat towards fishermen mending nets on the sand.

c3.title: Planning tank seams in Hayes
c3.text: Jodian is planning the back gouging of 12 m of double-sided butt welds in 16 mm plate on a large water-storage tank being built in Hayes, Clarendon. Trials show that with 6.4 mm electrodes the gouge advances at about 500 mm per minute. From past jobs, the gouger's arc is on for only about 30% of the working time, because of changing electrodes, grinding, moving and checking.

c4.title: An irrigation branch near Santa Cruz
c4.text: Marlon must fit a 100 mm branch (114.3 mm outside diameter, 6 mm wall) at 90° into a 200 mm main (219.1 mm outside diameter) for an irrigation scheme near Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. The drawing shows a set-in (set-through) branch. The site has oxygen and LPG cylinders, but no acetylene.

c5.title: Gussets and strips in Morant Bay
c5.text: Kerry-Ann's team at a shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas, must cut 40 gussets, each 250 mm × 180 mm, from 16 mm plate with a hand torch run against a template. A trial cut shows that the offset from the template edge to the centre of the cut, allowing for half the kerf, is 10 mm. They also cut long 40 mm wide stiffener strips from the edge of a plate. Some cut faces show strongly curved drag lines and bottom corners that are not cut through; others have a rounded top edge with beads of melted metal.

questions.q: How should Romaine connect the DC machine for gouging this carbon steel?
o: DC electrode positive (DCEP)
DC electrode negative (DCEN)
Either way round, as it makes no difference
AC, so the electrode wears down evenly
questions.why: Air carbon arc gouging of steel with copper-coated DC electrodes is normally done on DCEP. Other metals may need other set-ups, so follow the electrode maker's chart.

questions.q: While gouging, the electrode glows red far back towards the torch and its copper coat strips back. What is the most likely cause?
o: The air pressure at the torch is set too high
The current is too high for the electrode size
He is travelling too fast along the line of the crack
The electrode is held too flat to the plate
questions.why: An electrode overloaded with current overheats along its length, so the copper burns back and it wears away fast. Set the current inside the chart for the size (or use a larger electrode) and reset the stick-out.

questions.q: The PT check shows the crack runs 30 mm further than can be seen at one end. How far should Romaine gouge?
o: Only the 120 mm that can be seen by eye
To the end of the PT mark, and stopping exactly there
The full length shown, plus the procedure's margin
The visible length, then weld over the faint end
questions.why: Cracks are often longer than they look, and PT shows their true length. The excavation follows the whole indication and goes on past each end as the repair procedure says, so no crack tip is left to grow under the repair.

questions.q: The crack has been gouged out. What must happen before the repair weld?
o: Weld it straight away while it is still preheated
Wire-brush off the slag and start the repair weld at once
Paint the groove with primer to stop it rusting
Grind the groove clean and check it again with PT
questions.why: Grinding removes the carbon-rich, possibly hard surface left by gouging, and a second PT check proves no part of the crack remains. The preheat is then restored before welding.

questions.q: What is the most likely reason the slag stays in Fabian's groove?
o: The damp sea air stops the arc burning properly
The long, thin hose loses pressure at the torch
The current is so high that it melts too much metal
The electrode is too thin for the 8 mm hull plate
questions.why: A long, small-bore hose loses pressure and flow once air starts moving, even if the compressor gauge looks right. Check the pressure at the torch with air flowing, and use a shorter, larger hose or move the compressor closer.

questions.q: How should Fabian deal with the 200 A machine and his 8 mm electrodes?
o: Run the 8 mm electrodes at 200 A and travel more slowly
Run the 8 mm electrodes with extra air pressure
Turn the machine's current dial past its top mark
Use a smaller electrode that suits a 200 A machine
questions.why: An 8 mm electrode needs at least about 250 A, so at 200 A it sticks and leaves carbon. A smaller electrode whose chart range the machine can supply (within its duty cycle) gives a clean groove; for 8 mm, a bigger machine is needed.

questions.q: What should Fabian do about the fishermen downwind of the boat?
o: Carry on: the breeze will carry the fume out to sea
Give them ear plugs and carry on with the work
Carry on, but gouge only in short bursts
Ask them to move clear first, and screen the area
questions.why: The breeze is blowing from the boat towards them, so fume, sparks and molten spray will reach them, along with the noise. People are moved clear and the area screened before gouging starts.

questions.q: Which hearing protection should Fabian wear while gouging?
o: Ear plugs only, since he works in the open air
Ear muffs only, and just when the arc is long
Ear plugs and ear muffs, worn together
None, as the noise only lasts a few minutes
questions.why: Air carbon arc gouging is often louder than 100 dB(A), which damages hearing quickly. Plugs and muffs together give the extra protection needed, indoors or out.

questions.q: About how long should Jodian allow for the gouging, including the time the arc is off?
o: About 24 minutes
About 7 minutes
About 40 minutes
About 80 minutes
questions.why: Arc time = 12 000 mm ÷ 500 mm/min = 24 minutes. With the arc on only 30% of the time, the working time is 24 ÷ 0.3 = 80 minutes.

questions.q: In what order should the back gouging and welding of the long seams be done?
o: In sections, gouging and welding in a balanced order
Gouge the full 12 m first, then weld it all in one run
Weld the second side first, then gouge the first side
From one end to the other, as fast as possible
questions.why: Working in sections in a planned, balanced order controls distortion, keeps the gouged groove from standing open to rust and dirt, and makes any preheat easier to hold.

questions.q: About what size hole should Marlon cut in the main for the set-in branch?
o: About 102 mm, the bore of the branch
About 114 mm, the branch's outside size
About 219 mm, the main's outside diameter
About 57 mm, half the branch's outside size
questions.why: A set-in branch passes through the wall of the main, so the hole must be the branch's outside diameter, 114.3 mm. A hole the size of the bore suits a set-on branch, which sits on top.

questions.q: How should Marlon hold the torch while cutting the hole for the set-in branch?
o: Parallel to the branch centre line, all the way round
Pointing at the centre of the main pipe at every point
Tilted 45° outwards, away from the centre of the hole
Square to whichever surface is nearest the nozzle
questions.why: The branch must slide through the hole. Cutting parallel to the branch centre line gives hole walls the branch can pass; a cut pointing at the main's centre makes the hole narrow towards the inside at its sides.

questions.q: What changes when the cutting is done with oxygen and LPG instead of acetylene?
o: LPG nozzles and fittings; a slower preheat and more oxygen
Acetylene nozzles are used, with the fuel valve opened wider
No change, as the flame and nozzles are just the same
The LPG is mixed with oxygen in its cylinder first
questions.why: LPG needs nozzles, regulators, hoses and arrestors made for it. Its flame is cooler, so preheating and piercing take longer, and it uses several times as much oxygen as acetylene.

questions.q: What size should the team make the gusset template?
questions.why: For an outside shape, the template is smaller than the part by the offset on every edge: 250 − (2 × 10) = 230 mm and 180 − (2 × 10) = 160 mm.

questions.q: What causes the faces with strongly curved drag lines and uncut bottom corners?
o: Travelling too slowly along the line
A preheat flame that is too strong
Travelling too fast along the line
A nozzle held too close to the plate
questions.why: When the torch moves faster than the oxygen can burn through, the bottom of the cut lags behind, so the drag lines curve back and the corners are left uncut. Slow down to a steady, correct speed.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the rounded top edges with beads of melted metal?
o: A cutting oxygen pressure that is too low
Preheat too strong, or nozzle too close
Travelling too fast along the cut line
A nozzle one size too small for the plate
questions.why: Too much preheat, or preheat cones held too close, melts the top corner before the oxygen cuts it. Turn the preheat down and set the nozzle height from the chart.

questions.q: How can the team stop the long 40 mm strips bowing as they are cut?
o: Cut each strip in two halves from the middle
Cut both edges at once, or leave tabs till last
Cool each edge with water as soon as it has been cut
Cut each strip more slowly to spread the heat
questions.why: A strip heated along one edge bows as that edge shrinks. Heating both edges at once with two torches, or leaving uncut tabs that hold it straight until the end, balances or resists the pull.

questions.q: Dwight must remove the heads of 200 rivets from an old steel railway bridge girder without damaging the plate. Which method suits this best?
o: Wash them off with a rivet-washing nozzle held almost flat
Cut them off with a normal cutting nozzle held upright to the plate
Gouge each one out to below the plate surface with carbon arc
Grind them off flush with a cutting disc held square
questions.why: Washing removes metal standing above the surface without cutting into the plate, and the shanks are then punched out. An upright cutting nozzle or deep gouging would cut into the girder.

questions.q: A gouging nozzle uses about 2 400 litres of acetylene an hour. Each cylinder holds about 7 000 litres. Using the one-seventh rule, how many cylinders must be joined on a manifold?
questions.why: Each cylinder can safely give about 7 000 ÷ 7 = 1 000 litres an hour. 2 400 litres an hour needs at least 2.4 cylinders, so 3 are joined on a manifold. Drawing too fast can pull acetone out of the cylinders.

questions.q: Flame-cut edges of some high-strength steel plates cracked when they were bent in a press. What would most likely have prevented this?
o: Cutting faster, so that less heat went into the edges
Cooling the cut edges with water straight after cutting
Bending the plates while the edges were still hot
Preheating for cutting, or grinding off the hard edge
questions.why: On high-strength steel the cut edge cools fast and can harden. Preheating as the procedure says slows the cooling, and grinding off the hardened layer removes it before bending.
